newsitem.title: USA: OPTIONS - Dlr/mark vols lose steam after uptick.
newsitem.headline: OPTIONS - Dlr/mark vols lose steam after uptick.

text.p: Implied volatilities for dollar/mark options lost steam by U.S. midsession after popping up overnight on a rally in the spot greenback to a 40-month high of 1.7465 marks, U.S. traders said.

Even though the dollar has been well supported in the 1.74-mark area and hovered fairly close to the high, the uptick in front-end volatilities has failed to maintain momentum or spill over to longer maturities, they added.
"People for a long time have expected the dollar to go higher against the mark...and it has done so so methodically, in a very boring way," said a dealer at a Wall Street bank.
Traders said the upward pressure in the shorter dates probably stemmed from some gamma short-covering by dealers who had gone short options in recent range-bound trading in spot.

Implied volatility for one-month dollar/mark stood at 8.2/8.5 percent in U.S. midsession trade, off early highs but up about 0.2 point on the day. One-year also shed minimal early gains and was unchanged at 9.0/9.3 percent.
Alan Revercomb, options strategist at I.D.E.A., agreed that dollar/mark volatilities were unlikely to surge all out as long as the dollar's climb remained slow and tentative-looking.
"Volatilities are certainly cheap and starting to look attractive, but so far they haven't paid off yet," he said. "It (spot) has been clawing higher in a mind-numbing pace."

He added that a break lower in spot was more likely to cause a substantial spike in volatilities than a higher dollar, "unless it (spot) can pull dollar/yen high enough to make it look like an overall dollar move."

He added that dollar/mark and dollar/yen could re-couple in one direction or the other if U.S. interest rates climb back on the market's agenda after this week's Federal Open Market Committee meeting and June employment report.
In dollar/yen, volatilities dipped as spot seesawed in the low- to mid-114 yen area. One-month implied stood at 10.5/10.7 percent, off more than a quarter point from Friday.

"In dollar/yen, dealer positions are still dictating volatility moves," Revercomb said, referring to banks' long positions in upside strike prices and shorts in downside strikes resulting from strong end-user demand for yen calls.

A fall in spot inflates the dealers' negative gamma exposure in the downside strikes and forces short-covering, while a higher dollar boosts gamma in the upside strikes, forcing dealers to unload excess volatility positions.

The demand for yen calls, evidenced in risk reversals -- the put/call pricing differential -- refused to wane despite the dollar's bounce. One-month 25-delta stood at 2.2/2.5 point in favor of yen calls, marginally below last week's peaks.
"Nobody wants to part with that (yen call) right now," the Wall Street trader said.

Because the dollar was near the upper end of recent ranges amid so much fear for the downside, traders said perception seemed to be that the higher the dollar, the worse the risk-reward ratio was for risk reversals sellers because the call strike prices for equivalent deltas would be rolled up.
